Keeping four answers alive instead of one
Greedy commits to the best token at every step and can never take it back. Beam search keeps the
best partial answers: each step every one of them proposes its
candidates are ranked by their TOTAL log-probability, and the best
go on. A token that looked second-best can win
words repeat, because an untrained model has no preference worth the name.

B · The search as a tree — beam search against greedy
Each column is a step; each box is a surviving beam’s newest token and the total log-probability of its whole sequence (higher is better,
is certain). Lines follow the parent pointers. At
the best of the pruned candidates are drawn grey. Orange is greedy: the single best token at every step. Green is the beam that is best when the
trace ends — it started from the SECOND-best first token, which greedy discarded at once.

text.tspan: a search, and a check that the cache is exact
greedy, sampling and beam search, compared
compares three strategies on the same sentences, so the effect of each is
visible side by side. The deep dives at the end take them apart.
a built-in check that the cache is exact
# no check: the cache did not exist
A cache is an optimisation, and an optimisation must not change the answer. The notebook proves it on its own
sentences every run; this page proves it on the untrained model’s
A trained run dropped a word
In a trained run of this notebook,
decoded sequence B as "the is sleeping peacefully" — "cat" missing — while greedy and sampling were right. The cause is most likely the line if not beams or
: break, which can stop before the longest (right) answer finishes. Deep dive
Better sentences from the same model: by keeping four candidates, beam search found a sequence

more likely (in log-probability) than greedy’s after only five steps — here in an untrained model, and by much more in a trained one, where one early word decides the rest. The cache makes it affordable:
, with a reorder that keeps every beam reading its own past.
